items.title: Newton's biggest theorem says integration and differentiation are inverses
items.claim: Define F(x) as the area under f from 0 to x. The derivative of F is f. Define G(x) as an antiderivative of f. Then integral from a to b of f dx = G(b) - G(a). Two operations that look unrelated are inverses.

options.text: Integration (continuous summation) and differentiation (instantaneous rate) seem like different operations — but they undo each other. This is one of the most surprising and powerful results in mathematics

items.reveal:
Two parts:

FTC Part I: If f is continuous on [a, b] and F(x) = integral from a to x of f(t) dt, then F is differentiable on (a, b) and F'(x) = f(x).

FTC Part II: If f is continuous on [a, b] and G is any antiderivative of f (so G'(x) = f(x)), then integral from a to b of f(x) dx = G(b) - G(a).

Geometric intuition for Part I: F(x) is area under the curve up to x. As x increases by a small amount dx, the area increases by approximately f(x) * dx — the height at x times the width dx. So dF/dx = f(x).

Why it's surprising:
- Differentiation computes a LOCAL rate at one point.
- Integration sums up TOTAL accumulated value across a range.
- The connection: knowing the total at every point tells you the rate; knowing the rate everywhere tells you the total.

Applications:
- Definite integrals become easy: find an antiderivative, plug in endpoints, subtract.
- Areas, volumes, work, charge, total amounts of accumulated quantities — all computable via antiderivatives.
- Differential equations: solving f' = g is equivalent to finding an antiderivative of g.

Historical: Newton (~1665) and Leibniz (~1675) both discovered it independently. It's the cornerstone of mathematical physics.

Before the FTC, calculating areas under curves (the 'quadrature problem') was a major mathematical challenge — Archimedes computed parabola areas through laborious limit arguments. After the FTC, antiderivatives reduce the problem to algebra.
items.why: Calculus has two halves that look unrelated. The fundamental theorem reveals they are inverses — the same way logarithm and exponential are inverses. This unification is the most powerful idea in elementary mathematics.

items.title: 22/7 is a very good approximation of pi for a reason
items.claim: The fraction 22/7 = 3.142857 is closer to pi than its small denominator suggests. The fractions 355/113 = 3.141593 are even closer — accurate to 6 decimal places with only 6-figure numbers.
items.prompt: Why are these particular fractions so good?

options.text: They are 'convergents' of pi's continued fraction expansion, which generates the BEST possible rational approximations — no smaller-denominator fraction can be closer
They are products of pi's digits
All irrationals have such good approximations

items.reveal_title: Continued fractions and best rational approximations
items.reveal:
Pi's continued fraction expansion begins: 3 + 1/(7 + 1/(15 + 1/(1 + 1/(292 + 1/(...))))). The 'convergents' formed by truncating give:
3/1, 22/7, 333/106, 355/113, 103993/33102, ...

Each convergent is the best rational approximation to pi for its denominator size (no fraction with a smaller or equal denominator is closer). This is a theorem of continued fractions.

The large coefficient 292 in pi's expansion is why 355/113 is so good — it means the next convergent, after 355/113, only kicks in at much larger denominators. So 355/113 is unusually accurate for its size.

The golden ratio phi has continued fraction 1 + 1/(1 + 1/(1 + ...)), all 1s — making it the irrational hardest to approximate by rationals. This 'most irrational' property is why phi appears in plant phyllotaxis and quasicrystals.

Diophantine approximation studies exactly how well an irrational can be approximated by rationals. Roth's theorem (1955) gives sharp bounds for algebraic numbers; the field overlaps with number theory at every turn.
items.why: Approximating irrationals feels like it should give roughly similar fractions. Continued fractions give a precise algorithm for the BEST approximations and reveal why some irrationals are 'harder' than others.

items.title: Computers compute sine by adding up polynomials
items.claim: Your calculator can't 'compute sine'. It computes a polynomial that approximates sine very accurately. Specifically, sin(x) = x - x^3/6 + x^5/120 - x^7/5040 + ... The Taylor series gives any function as a sum of polynomial terms.

options.text: Polynomials and sine are always equal
Any analytic function f(x) can be expressed as a power series sum of f^(n)(a) * (x-a)^n / n!; truncating to a few terms gives a polynomial approximation with rigorously bounded error near x = a
Only sine has a Taylor series

items.reveal:
Taylor series: f(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + f''(a)(x-a)^2/2! + f'''(a)(x-a)^3/3! + ...

For analytic functions (most functions arising in physics and engineering), the series converges to f(x) within a radius of convergence around a.

Key examples around a = 0 (Maclaurin):
sin(x) = x - x^3/3! + x^5/5! - x^7/7! + ... (converges for all real x)
cos(x) = 1 - x^2/2! + x^4/4! - x^6/6! + ... (converges for all real x)
e^x = 1 + x + x^2/2! + x^3/3! + ... (converges for all real x)
ln(1+x) = x - x^2/2 + x^3/3 - ... (converges for |x| < 1)
1/(1-x) = 1 + x + x^2 + x^3 + ... (converges for |x| < 1, geometric)

For small x, truncating after a few terms gives good approximation. For sin(x), keeping x - x^3/6 gives error of about x^5/120; for x = 0.1, error ~ 10^(-8).

Calculators use TWO TRICKS:
1. Argument reduction: reduce sin(x) for large x to sin(x') where x' is in a small range, using periodicity and symmetries.
2. Polynomial approximation: minimax polynomials (Chebyshev-optimal) often beat Taylor for fixed precision.

Applications:
- Computer hardware (FPUs): implement transcendental functions via polynomial approximation.
- Numerical analysis: many algorithms (Newton-Raphson, Runge-Kutta) involve Taylor expansion.
- Physics: small-angle approximations (sin x ≈ x, cos x ≈ 1) are first-order Taylor.
- Perturbation theory in quantum mechanics: expansion of solutions around exactly-solvable cases.

Divergent Taylor series: some functions have Taylor series that converge only at a single point (formal series that don't represent the function). These appear in asymptotic analysis (Stirling's approximation, certain physics calculations).
items.why: Functions like sine seem 'analytical' or special. Computationally, they're polynomial approximations. The Taylor expansion is the practical universal interface between abstract functions and computers.
